outcomes: Map a one-output linear model to the course's row-major dense convention
Distinguish one-row predict from scalar and threaded batch-prediction wrappers
Return loss and parameter derivatives together from scalar and parallel fused APIs
Reduce private worker sums in fixed order and divide once by the complete batch size
Run actual parallel training with one simultaneous update

partition.name: Partition
partition.definition: A division of a workload into disjoint pieces whose union covers the original work.
partition.explanation: Batch rows can be partitioned because every row uses the same read-only parameters and produces its own prediction. Correct half-open ranges contain each row exactly once, including a shorter final shard when division is uneven. A partition is more than a chunk size: it defines ownership. Parallel prediction assigns disjoint output slices; training assigns private gradient buffers. The parent combines only after every worker completes.

scoped-thread.name: Scoped thread
scoped-thread.definition: A thread whose lifetime is bounded by a scope that joins it before returning.
scoped-thread.explanation: Rust scoped threads may borrow stack-owned slices and models because the scope guarantees those references outlive every worker. This avoids cloning large inputs or adding reference counting solely to satisfy a 'static requirement. The guarantee covers lifetime, not numerical correctness: code must still partition mutable outputs without overlap, handle worker panics deliberately, and choose enough work to justify thread creation and joining overhead.

gradient-shard.name: Gradient shard
gradient-shard.definition: A private parameter-gradient sum accumulated by one worker over its assigned examples.
gradient-shard.explanation: Each training worker starts a zeroed Gradient, visits its rows in fixed order, and accumulates a loss sum plus weight and bias derivative sums without synchronization. Gradient is derivative data in f64, separate from the Model's learned f32 parameter storage. The parent combines all shards and divides once by the complete batch size, including when the final shard is shorter. Private shards avoid races and hot locks while making reduction order explicit.

deterministic-reduction.name: Deterministic reduction
deterministic-reduction.definition: Combining partial results using a fixed grouping and order independent of worker completion timing.
deterministic-reduction.explanation: Floating-point addition rounds and is not associative. If workers update a shared sum in scheduler order, repeated runs can differ even when a mutex prevents races. This project stores partials by shard index and reduces them in ascending order. That gives scheduling-independent results for a fixed partition and build. It does not promise bitwise equality across thread counts, CPUs, compiler flags, vector widths, or fused operations; those can change grouping or rounding.

checks: predict_batch_parallel matches predict_batch for every row
loss_and_gradient_parallel agrees with scalar loss_and_gradient within tolerance
Workers return sums and 31 rows split across three unequal shards are divided by 31 exactly once
Three-shard training on 31 rows lowers MSE by at least 1000 times
Empty prediction succeeds while empty training, zero threads, and invalid shapes fail
limitations: Operating-system threads are created for each call rather than retained in a pool
Private gradients require one parameter-sized buffer per shard
Fixed-order reduction is reproducible only for a fixed partition, build, and target
The synthetic linear fixture validates mechanics rather than held-out generalization
